# Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire

## The document-object-model pattern

A striking share of serious S7 usage models **documents**: a map style, a
STAC catalog, a YAML configuration, a conversation transcript, a SQL
statement, a typed program awaiting compilation. A document is a nested,
typed, serializable *value* — declarative data with internal laws — and the
recurring architecture for it deserves a name and an explicit anatomy:

- **A class graph mirroring the document's semantic structure.** Composition
  edges (a style *contains* sources and layers; a catalog *contains*
  collections which contain items) become nested S7 properties. The graph is
  a tree of ownership.
- **Symbolic cross-references layered on the tree.** Documents routinely
  encode relationships the tree cannot: a layer references a source *by id*;
  an item links to a collection *by key*. These are relational edges embedded
  in a hierarchical format — effectively foreign keys — and they generate the
  referential-integrity invariants (every reference resolves; ids are unique)
  that belong to an aggregate-root validator, per the ladder in
  [04-parse-dont-validate.qmd](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd).
- **An aggregate root as the unit of consistency.** Following Eric Evans:
  outsiders hold the root; all modification flows through it; its validator
  is the lowest point that sees every cross-object law. The root is also,
  naturally, the unit of serialization and of external validation.
- **Boundary constructors that lift native objects into the model.**
  stacbuildr's `item_from_terra()`, `items_from_sf()`, and lidR bridges are
  the pattern in its clearest form: users hold rasters and geometries, and
  the package parses those *native* objects into document nodes at the
  boundary, rather than asking users to hand-assemble metadata.

## Documents are programs; your package is a front-end

The deepest reframe available for this pattern: a declarative document is a
**program** in a language you do not interpret. A map style is executed by a
rendering engine; a STAC item is executed by search tooling; a SQL string by
a database; a prompt-with-tools payload by an LLM provider. The R package
producing such documents is therefore a **compiler front-end**: its job is to
construct programs that are *well-formed by construction*, enforce the static
semantics that are cheap and local (the ladder, rungs 1–6), and delegate full
conformance to the engine's own authority (rung 0).

This framing settles several recurring debates at once. Should the model
validate everything the spec says? No — front-ends do not re-implement the
runtime; the official validator owns full conformance. Should documents be
built by string templating? No — compilers build structured representations
and serialize once, because templates cannot enforce structure. Is
hand-editing generated output acceptable? No — you do not patch a compiler's
output; you change the source and regenerate. And the imperative/declarative
boundary becomes crisp: the *document* is declarative (what should exist);
the *pipeline* that fetches inputs, builds it, writes it, uploads it is
imperative shell around a functional core, per
[02-values-and-state.qmd](02-values-and-state.qmd).

## Schema-driven development: postures toward an external schema

Most documents come with a schema — JSON Schema, a TypeScript definition
file, an OpenAPI component set, protobuf. Three postures toward *consuming*
one recur, and mature designs usually combine the first two; a fourth
relationship, pointing the opposite direction, appears when the model itself
is the source of truth.

**Schema as boundary contract.** Validate wire input and output against the
schema, mechanically, using the schema ecosystem's own tooling. S7schema is
this posture productized: YAML configuration in, AJV validation against JSON
Schema via V8, and only then S7/list objects out for downstream typed
extension. stacbuildr validates against the published STAC schemas. The
posture is cheap, authoritative, and evolution-friendly (schema versions are
explicit). Keep it wherever tooling exists.

**Schema as design input.** Read the schema as *evidence about the domain*:
census which property shapes recur (how many enum fields, how many bounded
numbers, how many string-or-expression slots), which fields are required,
where the sum types hide (`oneOf` with a discriminator), what is genuinely
extensible (`additionalProperties`). Then design the semantic layer —
atoms, composites, variant families — *informed* by the census but organized
around meaning. This is data-driven design in the first sense of
[03-types-and-meaning.qmd](03-types-and-meaning.qmd), and it is where design
quality is actually determined.

**Schema as codegen source.** Mechanically emit one class per schema object.
This is the tempting posture and almost always the wrong one, for a reason
worth stating carefully: **schemas encode structure, not semantics.** A
TypeScript interface file will happily contain fifteen interfaces that are
structurally distinct but semantically one concept (a color, expressed
fifteen ways), and zero indication of which nesting is a real domain object
versus a serialization artifact. A 1:1 mirror faithfully imports the
structure while discarding the one thing a domain model adds — meaning — and
saddles you with a class count that tracks the schema's quirks forever. What
*does* mechanize well is the regular substrate: enum value tables, wire-name
maps, requiredness matrices, version constants. Generate tables, not class
graphs; hand-design the classes from the census.

One legitimate exception deserves its own name so it stops being argued case
by case: the **generated transport model**. When faithful transport is
itself the requirement — an API surface too large and too churn-prone to
hand-model, consumed mostly by code generators downstream — mechanically
generated wire types are appropriate, *provided they are labeled as
transport* and kept behind boundary parsers that lift them into the
hand-designed domain layer (domain-driven design calls this arrangement an
anti-corruption layer). The two models coexist: generated types absorb the
schema's churn; semantic types carry the meaning. The anti-pattern was never
generation itself — it is mistaking the generated transport model for the
domain model, which is what "schema cosplay" names.

**The reverse arrow: schema as projection.** The three postures above concern
*consuming* an external schema. There is a fourth relationship, pointing the
other way: when the domain model is the source of truth, the schema is one of
its *outputs*. This only becomes possible under a specific precondition —
**constraints must be stored as data, not encoded as closures.** A validator
function can enforce a range but cannot be asked what the range is; a spec
object carrying `minimum` and `maximum` fields can do both. rtemis is the
fully developed exhibit: its property factories attach a `PropertySpec` object
recording type, bounds, enum, nullability, container shape, and a dozen
further axes as plain data, and from that one declaration the package
mechanically derives the R validator, the default, a JSON Schema (via
`S7_to_JSONSchema()`), and a TUI configuration form. sqlr is the same arrow in
SQL: the schema value renders to per-dialect DDL, compares structurally, and
diffs — projections a bag of `CREATE TABLE` strings could never support. The
payoff in both cases is the single-source-of-truth guarantee: the validator
and the published schema *cannot* disagree, because both are projections of
one datum. When you find yourself writing a validator and separately
documenting its rule, that is the signal this arrow wants to exist.

A compact translation guide from external constructs to S7 mechanisms:

| External construct | S7 mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| `const` / literal type | class identity: computed property or serializer-injected constant |
| `enum`, closed | validated character property (or a formalized enum class) |
| `enum`, extensible | validated character property plus a parse-boundary version gate |
| `oneOf` with discriminator | abstract parent + subclass family; the tag is class identity |
| `oneOf` of primitives | `S7::new_union()` on the property |
| `allOf` / interface extension | composition first; a parent class only if is-a is honest |
| `additionalProperties` | a pass-through bag property with key discipline only |
| nullable / optional | `NULL` union member + explicit presence policy (four axes) |
| nested object | composed S7 class |
| array of typed objects | list property with a membership validator |

## Serialization: one pair of functions knows the wire

Serialization discipline compresses to a single rule: **exactly one place in
the package knows what the wire looks like** — a `to_wire()` projection and a
`from_wire()` parser, usually generic-dispatched over the class graph.

The projection owns: wire-name mapping (`source_layer` → `"source-layer"`),
the omit-empty policy per field (absent key versus `null` versus `[]`, per the
presence axes of [03-types-and-meaning.qmd](03-types-and-meaning.qmd)),
injection of identity constants (version numbers, type tags), and recursive
descent through composed objects. The parser owns: version gating, coercion
into canonical representations, the unknown-key policy, and construction
through the front door so every law is checked on entry.

Round-tripping is a **law**, not an aspiration: `from_wire(to_wire(x))`
should equal `x`, and `to_wire(from_wire(doc))` should preserve every field
you claim to preserve. State the law, test it against gold files, and where
the round trip is deliberately lossy (normalization collapses equivalent
forms), document the quotient explicitly. This is the most valuable single
test family a document package can have, because it exercises the entire
class graph, both boundary functions, and the presence policy at once.

Stating the law *precisely* requires naming the equivalence relation,
because "equals" hides four different contracts: **representational
identity** (`identical()`, byte-for-byte); **canonical equality** (equal
after normalization to the one stored form); **semantic equivalence** (equal
ignoring non-meaningful variation — ordering, auto-generated names,
whitespace); and **wire equivalence** (equal once omitted fields and
defaults are resolved). Each round-trip promise should say which relation it
uses, and for most document systems the honest law is canonical equality,
not identity. sqlr models the discipline: its `sqlr_equal()` implements
semantic equivalence — constraints matched on what they constrain rather
than their order or auto-generated names — and its README says so
explicitly, which is what makes a hand-written schema comparable to a
reflected one.

Two packages show how far the round-trip law scales as an organizing idea.
sqlr's counterpart to `from_wire()` is `sqlr_reflect()`, which reads a *live
database's* catalog back into the same schema representation the renderer
consumes; the README calls the resulting equality "the package's own test
oracle," and makes it meaningful by defining equality structurally —
constraints matched on what they constrain rather than on order or
auto-generated names, so a hand-written schema compares equal to a reflected
one. typedjson goes further: the round trip is not a test of the product, it
*is* the product — faithful, human-readable JSON for R values, achieved by
annotating only what JSON cannot natively express (integer versus double,
typed missing values, non-finite numbers, attributes, objects from the S3, S4,
and S7 systems). Its design rule — keep ordinary JSON for ordinary values and
add the minimum machinery that makes the identity hold — is presence policy
elevated to a format's founding principle.

One structural decision deserves early attention: **open versus closed
nodes.** Foreign documents may carry extensions you do not model. A closed
node rejects unknown keys (maximal law enforcement, brittle against spec
evolution); an open node carries them through in a pass-through bag
(round-trip fidelity for foreign content, weaker guarantees). Real formats
need both, chosen per node — strict where you claim semantics, permissive
where the format is deliberately extensible (metadata blocks, vendor
extensions). What does not work is deciding by accident.

## Expression languages and the AST escalation ladder

Documents frequently embed a second, smaller language: filter and styling
expressions inside map styles, query fragments, template strings, tool-call
schemas. The design question — how much structure to give the embedded
language — has a clean escalation ladder, and the discipline is to **climb
only when the next rung's analysis is actually needed.**

**Rung 1: opaque passthrough.** The expression is a list (or string) the
model stores and emits verbatim; the engine's validator is its only judge.
Zero modeling cost, zero analysis capability. This is the correct *default*,
and treating it as the default is what prevents the most seductive
over-engineering in document modeling: rebuilding the engine's expression
type system in validators, forever, badly.

**Rung 2: constructor combinators.** Functions that *build* correct
expressions — `expr_match(field, cases)`, `expr_interpolate(...)` — giving
ergonomics, spelling safety, and partial static checking at construction
time, while the representation stays the wire's own (lists). This is a
*shallow embedding* of the foreign language: the combinators are the DSL, and
they compile immediately to the target form. Most packages should stop here;
it captures the bulk of the value (humans stop hand-writing nested lists) at
a fraction of the cost.

**Rung 3: a typed AST.** Node classes for the expression language, generic
passes over them — type checking, optimization, translation to *multiple*
targets. This is a *deep embedding*: the program is data (S7 objects), and
interpretation is a separate, swappable step. It is exactly what quickr is —
R functions with `declare(type())` annotations parsed into a typed S7
intermediate representation (typed nodes for subroutines, operations,
analyses), passes over that IR, and Fortran emission at the back —, and what
dbplyr does for SQL in S3 terms. The rung is justified when analysis or
multi-target translation *is the product*; it is pure cost when the only
consumer re-serializes to the single original wire format.

The general lesson generalizes past expressions: **representation should be
as deep as your analysis, and no deeper.**

## DSLs and metaprogramming: R's home turf, with guardrails

R is unusually good at embedded DSLs — quotation (`quote()`, `bquote()`),
first-class environments, lazy evaluation, and rlang's quasiquotation make
building little languages almost frictionless, which is precisely why
restraint is a design skill. Two patterns earn their keep in object-system
work:

**Checks as data.** Validator logic represented as composable *quoted
expressions*, assembled by a single function-builder into ordinary,
inspectable validator functions (`rlang::new_function()` over a spliced
body). This is a micro deep-embedding of a checking language, and it solves a
real problem — validator factories that call validator factories accumulate
argument-forwarding bugs; flat quoted checks compose without nesting. The
guardrails: generated functions must be *inspectable* (printing the body
shows exactly the checks, in order), *directly testable* (call the generated
validator in tests, not just the factory), and built by splicing quoted
expressions — never by `eval(parse(paste0(...)))`, which abandons hygiene,
tooling, and safety at once.

**Classes as data.** Because S7 classes are first-class values
([01-object-systems.qmd](01-object-systems.qmd)), factories that *return
classes* are ordinary code: an enum-class factory stamping variants from a
character vector (the s7x pattern), a family generator producing parallel
node classes from a table. The same guardrails apply, plus one more: generate
*structural regularity* only. The moment generated classes need per-class
special cases, the generator has become an obfuscation layer over what should
be ordinary, readable class definitions.

Both patterns assume the quoted material originates *inside the package*.
The moment expressions, extension bags, or class metadata arrive from
outside — a file, a wire, a user — the concern changes from hygiene to
security, and the rules harden: never evaluate untrusted text or quoted
structures; treat deserialization as parsing (rung 1 of the checking
ladder), never as object restoration by fiat; keep pass-through extension
bags inert data until something explicitly chooses to interpret them; and
bound recursion depth and payload size before walking untrusted nested
structures, because a parser that recurses on hostile input is a denial of
service waiting for its input.

The boundary that keeps metaprogramming honest is the one this whole
document has been drawing: **mechanize the regular, hand-write the
meaningful.** Wire-name tables, enum catalogs, repetitive property shapes —
generate. Domain concepts, invariants, the verb vocabulary — write, by hand,
where readers will look for them.
